7.text: While travelling in the country of Omolon and on both Anui rivers, I

8.text: found drums half worn-out on every dwelling-site of the former inhabitants,

9.text: who were starved out in the first decades of the nineteenth century, because

10.text: the wild reindeer almost ceased their yearly wanderings in that country. My

11.text: fellow-travellers, who were Russianized natives from the Kolyma country, felt

12.text: very uneasy on account of this abundance of drums, and repeatedly insisted

13.text: that the people must have been great sorcerers, and that it was no wonder

14.text: that God took them away from this world. These drums, however, were

15.text: only the old family belongings, which probably were used in a way similar

16.text: to that peculiar to the Chukchee.

17.text: Besides this general resemblance, it is difficult to say whether the sha-

18.text: manism of the neighboring tribes had any direct influence on that of the

19.text: Chukchee. The latter, indeed, treat “alien” shamans with as much veneration

20.text: as they do their own. In the western part of the territory of the reindeer-

21.text: breeders, many people apply to the Tungus shamans for advice, and some of

22.text: the Chukchee go so far as to procure for their own use large drums of the

23.text: more southern type employed by the Tungus.³

24.text: The old women of the Keˊrek tribe have the reputation of being very

25.text: skilful in working spells, and this skill is mentioned even in tales.⁴ The

26.text: shamans of the American Eskimo of the nearest shore of Alaska also enjoy

27.text: the respect of their Asiatic neighbors, both Maritime Chukchee and Asiatic

28.text: Eskimo. In one tale a contest between two shamans — one an American,

29.text: one an Asiatic — ends with a full victory for the American, although the

30.text: shaman from the Asiatic shore resorts even to treachery, and is severely

32.text: The direct influence of “alien” shamanism on the shamanism of the

33.text: Chukchee may be traced only in the shamanistic garment, of which I shall

34.text: speak in the latter part of this chapter.

35.text: INDIVIDUAL SHAMANISTIC INSPIRATION. — In modern times the importance of

36.text: family shamanism is losing ground among all the tribes named, with the ex-

37.text: ception of the Chukchee, and there is a tendency of its being replaced on all

38.text: occasions by individual shamanism. Individual shamans among the Chukchee

39.text: are called “those with spirits” (eñeˊñɪlɪt, from eˊñeñ,⁶ “shamanistic spirit”).
